transcript: Welcome to another episode of Dr. Dr. The Podcast featuring your physician host today, Dr. Tom McGovern, where we and our guests discuss relevant health-related topics from an authentically Catholic perspective. Today, we're presenting another bonus episode dealing with coronavirus. We're normally heard on the EWT and Global Catholic Radio Network. This episode will be played on various podcast apps and at radimoradio.com forward slash doctor. Today our guest is going to be Senator Todd Young, the senior senator from my state of Indiana where I live. He's been a guest on the show in the past and he's giving us a 15-minute window today to interview him about things of interest we think to most Catholic listeners regarding coronavirus. We do not have the intention of being politically partisan. We're going to focus on some of the popular things that have been done by the federal government and try to get some insight into how people at the federal level are looking at managing the crisis not only currently but especially in the future. So I'll be back in a moment with Senator Todd Young to see what he has to say to you and to me here on Dr. Dr. Senator Todd Young, welcome to another episode of Doctor Doctor. I know you're incredibly busy working seven days a week for however long coronavirus has been around here. Thanks for being with us. The first question I want to ask really impacts doctors and patients and that's telemedicine. The federal government has relaxed a lot of rules. The privacy rules have been relaxed, not eliminated. Medicare and other insurers are now paying for visits by telehealth like in-person visits, which is good. And we are now allowed as physicians to see patients across state lines, also very good. So telehealth is growing by leaps and bounds. These changes were initially announced to be temporary. And I know many of my colleagues who I've talked to since we last talked last week have told me they would not be doing telehealth except for these changes. So my question to you is what are the odds that these changes will become permanent? Oh, I think there's a really strong possibility that a number of these changes will become permanent. We should not go back to life completely as normal. There are a lot of lessons that we're learning over the course of this pandemic. And we should identify those silver linings and raise them and change our practices. So I've been a big believer in telehealth prior to the pandemic. I saw the opportunities associated with it in normal times. But as we look to expand access and improve care and bring cost down. Naturally, we're going to have to incorporate some of the things we're doing right now into that broader picture. I was pushing for expanded broadband deployment prior to the pandemic hitting in part for the telehealth services. Of course, there are a lot of other reasons we should invest in broadband deployment, but I think we're going to have to continue to look at some of these payment structures we put in place and maybe even incorporate more into our medical curriculum as we teach doctors how to use telehealth and to leverage these services. That's an idea I had never thought of, but yes, medical students should learn how to do that. Well, I spoke yesterday and it really occurred to me. It was a dermatologist who is one of the most respected dermatologists in the state and he said, you know, Todd, it really took this pandemic in our shelter-in-place situation for me to recognize the possibilities. And frankly, to get the comfort level, he said, many of my customers were more comfortable with it than I was initially. But he will never go back to business as usual. So he should receive the compensation for that. And of course, we're going to have to put parameters around this sort of care. But I'm just very excited about the possibilities. And do you think there is bipartisan support for doing that? I do. I do. There may be some principal disagreement surrounding some privacy issues and some other matters, but we'll identify in that policy event diagram where we can find common ground and come up maybe not with perfect policies in the back end, but better policies, I believe. Can you share any stories of how you've seen some of the legislation that you passed in a bipartisan fashion help either medical practices or small businesses? Well, as you know, many medical practices are small businesses. Exactly. And remain so, despite the consolidation we've seen across much of the medical industry. So Congress has really taken extraordinary steps to protect those enterprises during a time when otherwise it wouldn't have the capital to make payments for mortgages and rent and utilities and keep their workforces attached. The Paycheck Protection Program in particular has been very popular here in the state of Indiana. In fact, just the first round of funding led to $7.5 billion of loan approval in the state of Indiana. Most of that was directed towards small businesses. The national average for loan amount was roughly $200,000. The average loan was here in the state of Indiana, roughly 150, if I recall, and much of that's $50,000 or less. So we're talking about small, small bridge loans that disproportionately benefit those, for example, small optometry offices in Jennings County, Indiana, that's an echo example, and others who rely on this money just to pay their employees. It helped us bring 40 of our staff back with the PPE. So no, huge, huge for us. What do you think we as a nation and 50 individual states have learned that will be better off in the fall if there is an increase in numbers of COVID cases? Well, this is why we need a smart reopening of the economy to avoid the risk of you know, another spike in cases of COVID-19. And I commend Governor Polcom for allowing his public health counsel, his state Department of Health and the commissioner to really inform his policy responses. And we're trying to do that at the federal level as well. So the emphasis we're placing on testing and where possible contact tracing and putting protocols around different types of workplaces so that people feel safe and can go back to work and can resume some semblance of normalcy is really important. I also think that our public leaders emphasis on washing your hands and wearing masks in certain settings is something we're going to have to continue to be vigilant about. And there's been a lot of leadership shown on that front. It's not just government officials. I use the term leader broadly to encompass really everyone who can through modeling positive behavior impact in a positive way, the behavior of others. What is your understanding of the availability of testing now compared to a month ago? Are they pumping out more? Yes, my understanding is the trend lines continue to go up as manufacturing capacity is utilized as new manufacturing capacity is identified as some new tests are approved and developed. And as inputs for those tests, the ingredients for the tests, the reagents and other things and swabs are procured. So the trend lines are still up and that of course gives us more clarity about the health situation across different geographies and will allow us to get back to work even sooner in a helpful way, which is what we all want. Do you think that if there is an increase in cases in the fall will be unlikely we'll have to have the degree of shutdowns that we've had now in the spring? Well, I think we've learned a lot in the spring. In some of the exercises we've gone through, we probably won't have to repeat, right? I think that we may well determine that certain businesses that We're unable to open on account of the public health concerns have developed working rooms in the meantime and persuaded the public health community and our elected officials that those work around will protect workers, but still allow those businesses to provide the goods or services that they were providing so. That's an area that I know will be of continued interest and engagement for governors around the country and for the Trump administration. I'm working with the Trump administration on their opening up America Council and part of my role is to try and carry some of this information that's Indiana-specific. Do that committee and make sure that should this we get this reoccurrence in the fall, it'll be a little easier for us to adapt to it and frankly less costly in a lot of ways. Last week when we spoke, we found out we had a common interest in looking at the unintended consequences, medical consequences of all the shutdowns. For instance, at least past economic downturns have showed increases in suicide, drug use and overdose, domestic abuse, and poor health comes from people not seeking medical care when they needed to. You're obviously aware of this. How aware do you think other leaders in Washington are of the unintended consequences of things that aren't showing up on the dashboards of COVID cases and deaths? Well, not aware enough. I think most of my colleagues are certainly aware of the suicide cases we've had, but that's can be a factor loneliness can be a factor that absolutely impacts that. But it really doesn't encompass the much broader subjects of social isolation and loneliness. And there was a loneliness epidemic causing deaths of despair. It's been around for a number of years. Yes. But before the COVID pandemic hit, clearly. And you can't just legislate that away. So we're going to have to continue with this education effort. I like to say that the pandemic is creating sort of a national stress test for our country. Yes. In the course of that stress test, there's a magnifying glass that is shining on some of the existing stresses and vulnerabilities our country was already facing before the pandemic. This epidemic of loneliness is certainly one of those areas. So I'm trying to be constructive and provide some concrete responses to this, although much of the response needs to be at the neighborhood level, at the family household level, within churches. It's going to be non-governmental in nature. But I did just introduce legislation to make 988 the National Suicide Helpline. So that number needs to be as easy for most Americans to remember in dial as 911. And the state of Indiana just showed some leadership by launching a website, bewellindiana.org as a free resource. But I just go back to neighbors and not-for-profits and engaged citizens who love one another and care for one another as being the most important ingredient to address this loneliness epidemic. Yup, subsidiarity is a beautiful thing. What are the best bipartisan ideas you've heard about dealing with COVID going forward? Well, despite all the overheated rhetoric and histrionics that occur on cable news and talk radio oftentimes, almost all of our COVID response has been bipartisan in nature. We've passed four different bills or three and a half phases if you're really dialed into how we're talking about these things. And many of those bills passed unanimously. I mean, it's remarkable that we've dedicated these many resources towards this important priority. completed all the work in just a few weeks and passed much of it unanimously. And in the cases where there's been disagreement, the dissent has just been a couple of members. So I've really been encouraged by the sense of cooperation that pervaded Congress over these last few weeks. Cooperation is not an end in and of itself. There's a place for principled disagreement. There's a place for hate. But there's also a time to come together and come up with shared solutions to national problems that require immediate attention. And we've demonstrated that when push comes to shove, we really can get that done. And that's been encouraging to me and a lot of others. And last question, what do you think we should expect to see from Congress in the month of May related to COVID? Well, I think we will continue to make sure that these programs that we've been able to stand up to help small businesses and households so that they'll be made whole until they can get back to work will continue to improve their implementation. We want to make sure that they are accessible programs that people who require some assistance are getting that assistance. if there is replenishment of a particular program that is good public policy. And we'll fill a need out there. We'll do that. There may be some gaps in our response that we need to fill. And we of course want to make sure we do that. And then we're going to start to put Pen the paper relates to opening up the economy again and to the extent there are things at the federal level that we need to do. to facilitate that. We want to make sure that we're ensuring that people feel safe and informal, that allows people to go out there and not just meet their basic needs, but feel as though they're able to improve their circumstances if they work hard and play by the rules, which is where we were right before the pandemic hit. So we're going to work very hard to implement some policies that put us back on the path of rising wages and consumer optimism. Senator Todd Young, thank you so much for being with us on this episode of Doctor Doctor. Thanks a bunch for having me. I really enjoyed it, Doctor. explicit_propositions.text: Telehealth regulations have been temporarily relaxed by the federal government.
Medicare and private insurers now reimburse telehealth visits at rates comparable to in-person visits.
Physicians are now permitted to treat patients across state lines via telehealth.
Many physicians previously avoided telehealth due to regulatory restrictions.
Testing capacity for COVID-19 continues to grow due to increased manufacturing and procurement.
There is a high probability that key telehealth reforms will become permanent after the pandemic.
The Paycheck Protection Program provided $7.5 billion in loans to small businesses in Indiana.
A smarter reopening strategy emphasizes testing, contact tracing, and workplace safety protocols.
Congress has passed multiple bipartisan COVID relief measures, including several unanimous votes.
Average PPP loan size in Indiana was approximately $150,000, significantly lower than the national average.

assumptions.text: Policymakers value continuity and improvement in healthcare delivery beyond emergency conditions.
The benefits of telehealth—access, cost reduction, and efficiency—are sufficient to justify its permanence.
Economic stability depends on maintaining small business viability during crises.
Public trust in institutions improves when leaders demonstrate coordinated, evidence-based action.
Social well-being is intrinsically linked to physical health and cannot be ignored in public policy.
Bipartisan cooperation is feasible and desirable for addressing urgent national emergencies.
Government intervention is necessary to mitigate systemic risks affecting both health and economy.
Individual responsibility and community-level actions are essential complements to top-down policy.
Long-term societal resilience requires investments in infrastructure like broadband and mental health systems.
Catholic moral values align with public health priorities and responsible fiscal stewardship.
